summary: Specifies a Resource Directory, a service that stores information about resources on other servers so they can be looked up without direct discovery. This helps in Internet of Things networks with sleeping nodes or where multicast is inefficient. The document describes the web interfaces that servers use to register with it and that clients use to look things up.

eli5.summary: A phone book for tiny devices that sleep a lot, so you can find them without knocking on every door.

subtitle: A directory service where constrained IoT devices register their web links so others can look them up without waking or shouting at every device.

tldr.problem: In many IoT networks, asking each device directly what resources it offers does not work well, because nodes sleep and multicast traffic is inefficient.
tldr.mechanism: A Resource Directory (RD) stores links about resources held on other servers. Endpoints register and refresh their links over REST interfaces, and clients look them up through lookup interfaces that return web links.
tldr.outcome: Registrations are soft state with a lifetime, so entries expire unless refreshed. The RFC also defines security policy guidance, a new IPv6 Neighbor Discovery option for finding an RD, and several IANA registrations.

today: RFC 9176 is a Standards Track document (Proposed Standard, April 2022). It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it is the current specification of the CoRE Resource Directory.

sections.title: Why a Resource Directory
sections.content:
The Constrained RESTful Environments (CoRE) work established a REST architecture for constrained nodes and networks, used in Internet of Things and machine-to-machine applications such as smart energy and building automation. The CoRE Link Format of RFC 6690 describes how to discover resources by querying /.well-known/core on the server that hosts them.

That direct approach is not always practical. Nodes may be asleep, and on some networks multicast traffic is inefficient. A Resource Directory (RD) solves this: it holds information about resources hosted on other servers and allows lookups of them. The input to an RD is composed of links, and so is its output.

RFC 9176 specifies the web interfaces an RD supports for servers to discover the RD and to register, maintain, look up and remove information on resources. It also defines new target attributes useful with an RD. The examples use CoAP (RFC 7252), but the interfaces can be applied in an equivalent manner to HTTP.
sections.eli5: Tiny gadgets nap a lot, so shouting "who can do this?" to all of them does not work well. A directory lets them leave a note first, and you read the notes.

sections.title: Architecture and Content Model
sections.content:
An RD is a repository of registrations that describe resources hosted on other web servers, called endpoints (EPs). Endpoints use a registration interface to register, update and remove their registrations, and clients use a lookup interface to find the stored links. A Commissioning Tool (CT) can register on behalf of endpoints that are too constrained to do it themselves. An RD can be logically segmented using sectors.

Data in the RD can only come from the device that hosts the data or from a CT. Information SHOULD only be stored in the RD if it can also be obtained by querying the device's /.well-known/core directly. Changes in the RD do not propagate back to the original servers.

Each registration has an endpoint name (ep), a registration base URI (base), a lifetime (lt), a registration resource location (href), optionally a sector (d), and optional extra endpoint attributes. Registrations are soft state and must be refreshed periodically. The RD content model is described with entity-relationship diagrams.
sections.eli5: The directory keeps a card for each device with its name, how to reach it and how long the card stays valid. If the device does not renew the card, it gets thrown away.

sections.title: Finding the Directory
sections.content:
A device first needs the RD's address, then its URIs. A device may be configured with an IP address (possibly an anycast address) or a DNS name, or it may use DNS-based Service Discovery (DNS-SD). The RD advertises itself with the service names _core-rd._udp, _core-rd-dtls._udp, _core-rd._tcp and _core-rd-tls._tcp. Where nothing is configured, a network can offer a default through the new IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Resource Directory Address Option (RDAO), and as a last resort a device can try heuristics such as a multicast query. Multicast discovery in mesh networks is NOT RECOMMENDED. Because some guessed addresses will fail, endpoints MUST strictly rate-limit requests to candidate addresses that do not work.

The RDAO is carried in Router Advertisements, similar to the RDNSS option. It has Type 41, a Length that is always 3 (in units of 8 bytes), a Reserved field, a 32-bit Valid Lifetime in seconds (zero means the address is no longer valid) and the IPv6 address of the RD. Several RDAOs can be sent in one message.

Once a host is known, URI discovery is a GET to /.well-known/core with a resource type filter: rt=core.rd for registration, core.rd-lookup* for lookup, or core.rd* for everything. An RD MUST support the application/link-format content format (ct=40) and query filtering by rt.
sections.eli5: First you have to find the phone book itself. Maybe someone told you where it is, maybe the network shows you a sign, or you ask around. Then you ask the book which desk handles adding names and which handles looking them up.

sections.title: Registration and Maintenance
sections.content:
To register, an endpoint or CT sends a POST to the RD's registration URI with its links as the payload and query parameters: ep (endpoint name, unique within a sector, at most 63 bytes of UTF-8), optionally d (sector), lt (lifetime in seconds, 1 to 4294967295, defaulting to 90000, which is 25 hours) and base (base URI). The RD creates a registration resource and returns its location with 2.01 (Created). Registering again with the same ep and d replaces the earlier registration, so registration is idempotent. The base parameter is mandatory when a third party such as a CT fills the directory, or when the registrant uses an ephemeral port or cannot be reached at its source address (for example behind NAT).

Simple registration is for endpoints that cannot upload links. The endpoint sends an empty POST to /.well-known/rd, and the RD then fetches the endpoint's /.well-known/core to get the links. An RD MUST implement it, although it may be disabled for security reasons.

The location returned at registration is used for later operations. A POST to it with optional lt, base and extra attributes is an update, which resets the lifetime timer. A DELETE removes the registration, and the endpoint SHOULD do this when it knows it will no longer be available. If the lifetime expires, the RD SHOULD NOT answer discovery queries about that endpoint. If an update fails, the endpoint SHOULD register again.

Where security mechanisms allow reordering of requests, the RD needs to ensure request freshness. It SHOULD determine freshness and MUST use the CoAP Echo option of RFC 9175 if it requires freshness and cannot determine it otherwise.
sections.eli5: A device signs up once and gets a ticket number. To say "I am still here" it shows the ticket again. If it leaves, it hands the ticket back. If it just disappears, the ticket runs out on its own.

sections.title: Lookup
sections.content:
Clients find things with two mandatory lookup types, indicated by resource type: core.rd-lookup-res for resource lookup and core.rd-lookup-ep for endpoint lookup. An endpoint lookup MUST return a list of endpoints, and a resource lookup MUST return a list of links to resources.

Resource lookup returns links that are semantically equivalent to the ones registered, except that the target and any anchor are fully resolved against the registration's base URI. Endpoint lookup returns links to registration resources annotated with ep, d, base and the constant rt=core.rd-ep. The lifetime is not reported.

A lookup can carry several search criteria, and all of them MUST match. A criterion matches when a link has an attribute of the same name and value, with an optional trailing asterisk as a wildcard. The page and count parameters provide pagination: a count of 10 and page of 0 returns links 0 to 9, and page 1 returns links 10 to 19. Clients that want updates can use ETag caching or CoAP resource observation. If a registration's base URI is a link-local address, the RD MUST NOT show its links unless the lookup came from the same link.
sections.eli5: Looking something up is like asking the phone book for everything labeled "light". You can ask for the answer a page at a time, or ask to be told when something new shows up.

sections.title: Security Policies and Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not set one security policy, because it depends on the application. Section 7 lists aspects to consider: who may use which endpoint name, which links an endpoint may enter, link confidentiality, and segmentation of different policies by sector. It also gives a reference default called First Come First Remembered. The RD accepts a registration for any endpoint name not held by an active registration, and accepts later operations on it only from the same client, identified by subject name, public key or security session. Clients MUST be prepared to pick a different endpoint name if rejected.

The security considerations say that access that is limited or sensitive SHOULD be protected, for example with (D)TLS or OSCORE. Discovery is mostly not covered by CoAP security and can leak a client's intentions. Every operation by an endpoint SHOULD be mutually authenticated, and an endpoint MUST NOT be identified by protocol, port or IP address because those can change. The RD should check that the identity used at the security layer is allowed to use the endpoint name it claims.

Simple registration could be used to get around address-based access control, so the RD SHOULD verify the sender, for instance with the Echo option. RDs running over unprotected UDP can be abused for denial-of-service amplification because lookup responses can be much larger than requests. Access control SHOULD be separate for registration and lookup, and as fine-grained as possible.
sections.eli5: A phone book needs rules about who can write in it and who can read it. Otherwise a stranger could erase a neighbor's entry or put in a fake one.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has added resource type values core.rd, core.rd-lookup-res, core.rd-lookup-ep and core.rd-ep, and registered IPv6 Neighbor Discovery option type 41 for the RDAO. The RFC creates two new subregistries in the CoRE Parameters registry: "RD Parameters", whose initial entries are ep, lt, d, base, page, count and et, and "Endpoint Type (et=) RD Parameter Values", whose initial value is core.rd-group. Future additions to the RD Parameters subregistry use Expert Review.

Multicast addresses were assigned for "All CoRE Resource Directories": 224.0.1.190 for IPv4 and ff0x::fe for IPv6. The well-known URI suffix rd was registered, along with the service names core-rd (UDP and TCP), core-rd-dtls and core-rd-tls.
sections.eli5: The special names and numbers this system uses were written into the official lists, so nobody else uses them for something different.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in units of 8 bytes. Always 3.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Initialized to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: Valid Lifetime
fields.desc: Seconds this RD address is valid; zero means not valid anymore.
